listitem.para: Intracarotid amobarbital (Wada) test may be indicated when ALL of the following are present:
Noninvasive test (eg, functional MRI) results inconclusive regarding lateralization

Surgery planned (eg, temporal lobectomy for medically refractory epilepsy)
Intractable or medically refractory epilepsy is defined as seizures that are unresponsive to at least 2 different, tolerated, appropriately chosen, and used antiseizure medications.
Brain functional MRI. See Brain Functional MRI for further information.
Magnetoencephalography. See Magnetoencephalography for further information.

guideline-sect3.heading: Background
guideline-sect3.para: The Wada test is used to lateralize language and memory function in the cerebral hemispheres for preoperative evaluation of patients with planned temporal lobe surgery; however, most centers now perform functional MRI for this purpose. The test consists of catheterization of an internal carotid artery and injection of a short-acting anesthetic, traditionally amobarbital, that anesthetizes that hemisphere; after injection, the awake patient is asked language and memory function questions. Failure of a specific function during questioning points to the lateralization of that function. Because amobarbital availability has been a worldwide concern, methohexital, pentobarbital, secobarbital, etomidate, and propofol have been evaluated as viable alternatives, but risks and benefits should be considered on an individual basis.

guideline-sect3.heading: Criteria
guideline-sect3.para: The evidence for the clinical indications found in this guideline includes 19 published peer reviewed articles, 2 specialty society or other evidence-based guidelines, and 2 book sections.

For language and memory lateralization, evidence demonstrates a net benefit, but of less than moderate certainty, and may consist of a consensus opinion of experts, case studies, and common standard care. (RG A2) Review articles note that although the Wada test has been considered the gold standard for preoperative language lateralization, it is being increasingly replaced by other noninvasive tests, such as brain functional MRI and magnetoencephalography. However, the Wada test may be preferable if brain functional MRI results are inconclusive, if they indicate bilateral language localization, or if the patient cannot tolerate MRI. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of the Wada test for both memory and language lateralization found very low-quality evidence and significant study heterogeneity, limiting the ability to draw conclusions. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies (124 patients with temporal lobe epilepsy) found overall agreement for memory lateralization between Wada test and functional MRI of 46.8%; there was an association between disagreement between tests and bilateral memory lateralization. The limitations included heterogeneity of the protocols in the included studies and lack of clear postoperative memory outcomes standards; however, the authors recommended further study to evaluate the use of functional MRI in this population. A retrospective study of 141 first-time Wada test results found that right-handed patients with a right temporal lesion and strong verbal memory (ie, a cognitive profile consistent with a nondominant focus) are very unlikely to fail memory tests during Wada and probably do not need to undergo the test; in contrast, patients with left-sided temporal lesions are more likely to fail regardless of handedness and baseline neuropsychological test data. The authors concluded that until functional imaging protocols become available and accepted as an alternative to the Wada test, patients should be considered for the Wada test on a case-by-case basis. A retrospective study of 48 presurgical epilepsy patients identified several indications for Wada testing, including an inability to perform functional MRI (eg, due to agitation, mental or perceptual impairment); atypical, inconclusive, or not clearly lateralized language activation with functional MRI; need for selective testing of language and other cognitive functions; and need for motor localization.

guideline-sect3.heading: Rationale
guideline-sect3.para: Use of this MCG care guideline helps the clinician determine if a particular treatment, medication, or service might be appropriate for a specific patient, taking into account their unique health complexities.

Use of these evidence-based clinical criteria to support decision making benefits the patient by identifying patient-specific complex clinical factors and conditions, promoting personalized treatment. Utilizing evidence-based clinical criteria promotes patient safety by helping ensure that potential patient benefits outweigh the risks. In addition, the use of evidence-based guidelines can increase consistency in treatment thresholds, leading to less variation in care and promoting equitable treatment among patients.

guideline-sect3.heading: Related CMS Coverage Guidance
guideline-sect3.para: This guideline supplements but does not replace, modify, or supersede existing Medicare regulations or applicable National Coverage Determinations (NCDs) or Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs).
